author: Adel Ahmad
title: "Durant wanted an offense that kept the ball moving" - Kevin Durant felt Russell Westbrook's ballhogging tendency wouldn't ever allow him to win a title - NewsBreak
text: Kevin Durant had spent nearly a decade trying to make it work in Oklahoma City, but by the summer of 2016, he had run out of patience. Despite all the talent and sky-high potential, the Thunder kept coming up short. While many chalked up his departure to Golden State as a "soft" move, those closest to the situation knew there was a deeper frustration brewing behind the scenes, one that revolved around the Thunder's inability to evolve offensively. According to Bleacher Report, Durant had grown tired of watching the same patterns play out year after year. "Durant wanted an offense that kept the ball moving and provided him easier scoring chances," the report said . "The Thunder fired coach Scott Brooks, brought in Billy Donovan, and still the offense stalled out at key moments, often with Westbrook dribbling into oblivion." It wasn't a talent issue. Durant and Russell Westbrook were two of the most explosive scorers of their generation. They made four Western Conference finals and reached the NBA Finals in 2012, but the offense consistently sputtered in the clutch. In the 2015–16 season alone, the Thunder led the NBA in blown fourth-quarter leads with 14, a stat that summed up just how often they lost control of winnable games. Coach Billy Donovan was hired to bring something fresh to OKC after the front office moved on from Scott Brooks, but it quickly became clear that the new offense wasn't much different from the old one. The ball still stuck. Durant still had to work through multiple defenders to get shots, and Westbrook, no matter how dynamic he was, often caught backlash for his tendency to play out of control or shoot too many ill-advised shots. "Ultimately, he got frustrated and felt that they had plateaued," a source close to Durant told BR . "[Donovan] came in, and he still had the same issues that he had with Russ under Scotty. The offense didn't change much. He still had to take a ton of contested shots every game, and that's when he had the ball at all." Durant averaged 28.2 points on 50 percent shooting that season, but over 46 percent of his shots were tightly contested. He was often forced to isolate or create something out of nothing, even with Westbrook by his side. During the 2016 Western Conference finals, when the Thunder blew a 3–1 lead to Golden State, Durantula averaged 30 points but did so while shooting just 41.5 percent from the field in the final three games. Westbrook took nearly as many shots, and his usage rate remained one of the highest in league history for a point guard. That imbalance showed up in late-game breakdowns, stagnant halfcourt sets and Durant's increasingly visible frustration on the floor. KD had no problem deferring when the system worked, but when possessions devolved into one-on-one heaves and end-of-clock bailouts, he began to question whether he could ever win with Westbrook as his co-star. Related: "Both of them have the same DNA" - John Calipari on the unique trait Derrick Rose and Shai Gilgeous-Alexander share Durant's move to Golden State was about finding a system that actually fit. The Warriors' offense featured constant movement and unselfish play thanks to Stephen Curry and Klay Thompson, both of whom could — and still can — rattle off a 12 3-pointer game on any given night. Critics questioned the decision, but the results were undeniable. Durant won back-to-back titles and two Finals MVPs with the Warriors, averaging 29 points on nearly 53 percent shooting in the postseason. His time in OKC will always be remembered for the highs and heartbreaks, but the root of his exit came down to Kevin having seen enough of the isolation and the fourth-quarter meltdowns.
